disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention such as difficulty sustaining focus, disorganization, distractibility, and forgetfulness, without the prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors seen in other ADHD presentations. Symptoms must be developmentally inappropriate, present for at least six months, and cause clinically significant impairment in academic, occupational, or social functioning, with onset in childhood even if diagnosis is delayed until adulthood. The course is often chronic, though the way impairment manifests can change across the lifespan as environmental demands shift (e.g., transitions in schooling, job complexity, or caregiving roles). It is distinguished from anxiety and mood disorders by the pervasiveness and early onset of attentional difficulties, and from cognitive disorders by its stability over time and lack of progressive decline.

narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Shirley was promoted to oversee a larger service line, which dramatically increased her volume of meetings, strategic reports, and regulatory deadlines. For years she had compensated for long-standing attention difficulties with meticulous color-coded spreadsheets, late-night coffee-fueled work sessions, and over-preparation, but the new role demanded she juggle more simultaneous projects and rapidly switch between EPIC dashboards, budget models, and quality metrics. As her health system pushed through a major electronic record upgrade and COVID-related backlog initiatives, she began missing key follow-ups and struggling to keep track of complex initiatives despite putting in longer hours and tightening her routines at home. The growing gap between her reputation as a highly organized leader and her private sense of falling behind at work, coupled with feedback from colleagues about dropped balls, led her to seek psychiatric evaluation after her primary care doctor suggested her lifelong focus problems might reflect undiagnosed ADHD rather than simply stress or aging.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to stay focused long enough to get through all the reports and planning tasks my job requires anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Jason formally retired from paid handyman work a little over two years ago, shifting his time into structured volunteering as an arts liaison and planning workshops for seniors. Without the concrete, hands-on jobs and daily routines he had relied on for decades, he began noticing how hard it was to keep track of multi-step plans for gallery walks, lecture series, and his own photography projects, despite carefully written notes and printed maps. As he took on more responsibility coordinating volunteers and communicating with museum staff, he became increasingly frustrated by how often he would start organizing one event and then drift off into reading about art history or rearranging his photo archive, only to realize later that key tasks had been left incomplete. Concerned that his long-standing tendency to "zone out" was becoming more disruptive in this new phase of life, and worried it might signal early cognitive decline, he consulted his primary care physician, who then referred him for a psychiatric assessment to clarify whether his persistent difficulties fit an inattentive ADHD pattern rather than a neurocognitive disorder.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since I stopped working full-time, I keep starting projects for the museum and then just never finishing them, even when I really want to.”

narrative.stressor: After graduating with her humanities degree and taking on a full-time role at the meat processing plant, Clara moved from predictable student schedules into a fast-paced environment where she had to balance safety protocols, production targets, and mentoring new staff. Over the past two years, as she started training others and managing more of the workflow, her long-standing tendency to misplace tools, paperwork, and inventory logs began to affect line efficiency and drew attention from her supervisors. At the same time, she was trying to pursue extra certifications in sustainable sourcing, juggling dense reading materials and online modules on top of rotating shifts, and found it increasingly stressful that she kept having to replace or search for the same essential items during busy runs. After a near-miss incident where misplaced equipment briefly disrupted operations and embarrassed her in front of newer workers she was mentoring, she discussed her ongoing organizational struggles with a friend from college, who suggested that her lifelong scatter around materials might be part of undiagnosed inattentive ADHD, prompting her to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly losing the tools and paperwork I need at work, and it’s starting to cause real problems on the line.”
